brand.name: aicourse.top
brand.sub: Free, open courses to understand, use, build, and evaluate AI.
home.lede: Choose a course to understand AI systems, use today's tools, or build reliable workflows. Published courses show what you will make, how long they take, and how you will prove what you learned.
home.free: No account. No ads. Anonymous page counts only. MIT licensed.
home.heroAlt: An open book connected to course tiles for conversation, code, AI models, data and safety.
home.topicsTitle: What do you want to learn?
home.topicsLede: Start from your goal, not from a product name. You can switch paths whenever your work changes.
home.pathLede: Each part asks a little more of you than the last. Start at the top.
home.coursesLede: Pick the outcome that matters today. Each course stands on its own; the learning paths help when you want a sequence.
home.githubPoint1: Build a secure, reviewable repository in the browser
home.githubPoint2: Adapt issues, pull requests, Projects and releases to five work contexts
home.githubPoint3: Finish with a source-grounded assessment and auditable capstone
home.promptsPoint1: Turn vague requests into testable prompt contracts
home.promptsPoint2: Evaluate six representative cases, not one attractive answer
home.promptsPoint3: Finish with a reusable prompt evidence packet
home.agenticPoint1: Understand where models belong in a system
home.agenticPoint3: Build an agent with safety gates
home.claudePoint1: Choose the right Claude surface, context, tools, permissions, and review boundary.
home.claudePoint2: Practise source-grounded workflows for software, research, data, writing, office work, and teaching.
home.claudePoint3: Complete a six-artifact portfolio across Delegation, Description, Discernment, and Diligence.
home.pathsTitle: Follow a route, or make your own
home.pathsLede: Paths connect courses around a goal. They are recommendations, never locked prerequisites.
home.path1d: Build an accurate mental model before you reach for a tool.
home.path1b: Practise with a real model call
home.path1c: Build and evaluate a small agent
home.path2: Build with an AI coding partner
home.path2d: Move from a clear task contract to tested, reviewable code changes.
home.path2a: Ground the task in the repository
home.path2b: Implement and steer in small slices
home.path2c: Verify the diff and keep evidence
home.path3d: A growing route for research, writing, teaching and responsible use.
home.path3a: Frame a claim and its evidence
home.methodLede: The platform is designed around visible learning—not passive watch time or badges without evidence.
home.method1d: Interactive tasks make you choose, run and revise instead of only reading the answer.
home.method2d: Checks, sources and capstone artifacts make your progress inspectable and reusable.
home.method3d: No learner account is required. Progress stays in this browser unless you export it.
home.progressLede: Published courses save milestones locally so you can return without creating an account.
home.modulesLede: Read the model, practise the decisions, then build the loop yourself.
track.1.title: The Handbook
track.1.desc: Eleven illustrated sections on who decides the next step at run time — writing code, prompts, context, loops, graphs, harnesses, evaluation and security. Twenty diagrams you can click through.
track.2.title: The Lab
track.2.desc: Four hands-on stages in this browser. Make a real model call, extend a rule-based till until it breaks, write your own prompt, then score it against twenty real cases and watch the number move.
track.2.meta: 40 minutes · your own API key · about 1¢
track.3.title: Build an Agent
track.3.desc: Five more stages, on your own machine. The agent loop written by hand, tools that fail on purpose, a permission gate, a reviewer that cannot be skipped, and an email that tries to give your agent orders.
home.learnTitle: What you will be able to do
home.learn1: Tell which problems need a model and which do not
home.learn1d: The most valuable judgement in the field, and the cheapest to get wrong.
home.learn2: Write a prompt and prove it works
home.learn2d: Not by reading its answers — by scoring it against cases and watching a number.
home.learn3: Build an agent loop that survives failure
home.learn3d: Tools break. The loop has to read the error and adapt, not crash.
home.learn4: Put a fence around what a model can do
home.learn4d: Permission gates, mandatory review steps, and limits enforced in code.
home.for1d: Parts 1 and 2 assume no programming at all.
home.for2d: A full curriculum you can finish in an afternoon.
home.for3d: A 90-minute lesson plan, free to reuse and translate.
home.progNone: No course progress yet. Pick a course when you are ready — nothing is sent anywhere.
home.a1: Yes. Original course text and code are MIT licensed; separately attributed third-party assets retain their own terms. There is no account, email capture or advertising, and the site measures anonymous page views only. A few optional exercises call an external model with your own API key and explain any small token cost before you run them.
home.q2: Which course should I start with?
home.a2: If AI is new to you, start with the illustrated Handbook and browser Lab in Agentic Engineering. If you already work with code, you can begin directly with the Codex course. Learning paths are recommendations, not gates.
home.q3: Do I need to know how to program?
home.a3: No for the Handbook and Lab. Project courses clearly state when they require basic TypeScript, a code editor or command-line experience, so you can choose a course that fits where you are.
home.a4: Course milestones and your theme choice stay in this browser. There is no learner account. The site counts anonymous page views, but it does not receive your course progress or any API key you use in the Lab.
foot.licence: Original text and code are MIT licensed; third-party assets retain their listed terms.
foot.disclaim: Not affiliated with any AI provider. All model behaviour shown is as of the model you run it on.
lab.keyNote: Held in this browser tab only and erased when you close it. Sent to the model provider and nowhere else — your key never reaches this site's own analytics, which counts page views and nothing else.
note.englishOnly: The teaching text in this section is currently English only. The interface is translated into nine languages; translating the long-form articles is the next job, and contributions are very welcome.
note.langHelp: Spotted a bad translation? Corrections are welcome — every string lives in one file.

ab.title: About
ab.lede: aicourse.top is a free, open platform for practical AI learning, built by educational-technology researchers who study how people understand, use and evaluate new tools.
ab.teamLede: Researchers whose work shapes how these courses are designed and evaluated.
ab.why1: AI learning is often split between simplified explainers and product tutorials that assume too much. Learners need routes from first principles to real, reviewable work.
ab.why2: This platform keeps those routes free, open and accessible across nine interface languages. Agentic Engineering is one path inside a broader curriculum for using, building and evaluating AI.
ab.how1: Courses connect concise explanations to practice, evidence and explicit limitations. Tool-specific lessons preserve sources and review dates; project courses finish with something the learner can inspect or verify.
ab.how2: Everything is MIT licensed and public. If a claim, translation or exercise can be improved, the source is open for review and contribution.
ab.p.peter.aff: CEO and Founder, PedaNova Ed-Tech · Developer of 3D ENA 2.0
ab.p.peter.bio: Dr. Hu holds a PhD in Educational Technology from the University of Hong Kong and a BSc in Computer Science (machine learning and artificial intelligence) from the University of London. He builds theory-informed learning environments and analytical tools that connect educational research to working technology, and publishes in journals ranked among the top ten in Education and Educational Research by Web of Science. He wrote this course.
ab.p.hwang.bio: Prof. Hwang works on technology-enhanced learning: mobile and ubiquitous learning, game-based and flipped approaches, and artificial intelligence in education. His research links intelligent learning design to evidence-based teaching and assessment.
ab.p.tu.aff: National Taiwan University of Science and Technology
ab.p.tu.bio: Dr. Tu studies how generative AI and digital learning shape what learners perceive, do and achieve. She combines educational data mining, visual and network analysis, and mobile-learning research to make the process of learning visible enough to act on.
ab.p.yu.aff: 3D ENA Research Group, Hong Kong · BSc Computer Science, MA Psychology
ab.p.yu.bio: Mr. Yu brings together computer science and psychology to build interactive tools for epistemic network analysis and quantitative ethnography. He is the lead developer of 3D ENA 1.0, and applies network analysis to political discourse and social-media data.
lab.stepsLabel: The four steps of the Lab
lab.s1.name: Your first call
lab.s2.name: The wall
lab.s3.name: Write the prompt
lab.s4.name: Measure it
lab.nothingYet: The model's answer will appear here.
lab.setup.title: First, connect a model
lab.setup.lede: Three of the four steps below send your words to a real AI model and show you what comes back. For that the Lab needs a key of your own. It takes about two minutes, once.
lab.setup.whatIsBody: It is a long password that lets a program talk to an AI model on your behalf. You create one on the model provider's website, and it belongs to you, not to us. You pay the provider only for what you use — everything in this Lab costs roughly one cent.
lab.setup.s1d: Sign up, then add a small amount of credit. One dollar is far more than this course will ever use.
lab.setup.s2: Create a key and copy it
lab.setup.s2d: It is a long line of text beginning with sk-. Copy all of it — the site shows it to you only once.
lab.setup.s3: Paste it in the box below
lab.setup.s3d: It stays in this browser tab and is erased the moment you close it.
lab.keyPlaceholder: Paste your key here — it starts with sk-
lab.err.noKey: This step needs your API key, and none is saved yet.
lab.err.noKeyCta: Take me to the key box
lab.err.badKey: That key was not accepted. Check you copied all of it, with no spaces at either end.
lab.err.noCredit: The account behind this key has no credit left. Add a little on the provider's site, then try again.
lab.err.busy: The model is busy right now. Wait a few seconds and try again.
lab.err.network: The model could not be reached. Check your internet connection and try again.
lab.err.generic: That did not work. The provider's own words are below, in case they help.
home.ideaLede: Every program is a list of steps. The only question is who chooses the next one, and when.
home.ideaAd: You write the steps in advance. The computer follows them exactly, every time — fast, predictable, and blind to anything you did not think of.
home.ideaBd: You describe the goal and let the model choose the next step while the program is running. Flexible, surprising, and it has to be checked.
home.ideaFoot: Almost every real system is a mixture of the two. Choosing the mixture is the whole job — and it is what you will practise here.
track.3.note: Opens on GitHub. You will need a computer and a code editor.
lab.enData: The café orders, the menu and the twenty test cases stay in English. They are the exercise itself — the scoring compares the model's answers against English standards — so translating them would change what is being measured.
lab.s1.lede: Before anything clever: prove the wire works. Ask the model anything, and watch what it costs — almost every tutorial hides that number.
lab.s2.lede: A till built the ordinary way — a list of rules a person wrote in advance. **Add rules until it handles all ten phrasings.** Real customers wrote them. Nothing on this step talks to a model, so it costs nothing.
lab.s2.wall: **Look at what you had to write.** {rules} rules for ten sentences — and you had to think of each phrasing *before the customer did*. That is the wall. It is not a bug in your code; it is the shape of the problem.
lab.s3.lede: The same café till, but this time you describe the job in words instead of listing every phrasing. Write it, then try it on three real orders.
lab.s3.hint: You are the till at a small café…
lab.s4.lede: Three orders is a feeling. Twenty is a number. Run the whole set, then change one thing and watch the number move.
lab.s4.jump: **{prev} → {score}.** Same model, same twenty questions. The only thing that changed is that you told it what it was selling. **Most “the model is bad” is really “the model was never told”** — and you only know that because you had a number before and after.
lab.s1.q: Explain what an API is, to someone who has never written code. Two sentences.
